results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long to keep tax records?**  
*The periods you must keep records are based on the type of record and the tax rule that applies to it.*

| What you’re keeping | How long you need to keep it | Why |
|---------------------|------------------------------|-----|
| General business receipts, invoices, payroll, etc. – anything that backs up an item of income or a deduction on a return | Keep them **until the period of limitations for that return expires** – usually **the period after you filed the return that allows the IRS to add tax or you to claim a refund**. The standard limit is **3 years** from the filing date, but it can be longer for some situations. | The IRS can only amend a return or assess new tax within that period. If you have those records beyond the limit they’re no longer needed for IRS administration. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (e.g., W‑2s, payroll forms, payroll tax returns) | **At least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid (whichever is later)** | Employment‑tax law specifically requires a 4‑year retention. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Records for a property you own (depreciation, cost basis, disposition) | Keep them **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property**. | These documents are needed to calculate gain or loss and depreciation, and the period of limitations is tied to the year you sell or otherwise dispose of the property. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Records that might be needed for other purposes (insurance, lender requirements, etc.) | Do **not discard them until you’re sure no other agency or creditor requires them longer**. | The IRS says to keep records longer if another party demands it. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Records that support a claim for a **loss from worthless securities or a bad‑debt deduction** | **7 years** | This is a special exception to the normal 3‑year rule. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Records that support a **fraudulent return** or a return **not filed at all** | **Not limited** – keep them forever | The IRS can investigate fraud or non‑filing at any time. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Records for a **claim for a credit or refund** | **Later of 3 years after filing or 2 years after the tax was paid** | This is another special period that can be longer if the tax was paid later. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |

---

### How to decide which period applies

1. **Start with the type of record** (e.g., payroll, property, general business receipts).  
2. **Find the rule that matches** that type in the IRS instructions.  
3. **Use that rule’s time frame** – if the rule says “no limit,” keep everything. If it says “3 years” or “4 years,” that’s the minimum you’ll have to preserve the record.

If you are ever unsure, keep the records longer. Destroying them too early can create audit problems or make it harder to prepare future returns.  

**Summary:** Keep most business records for at least the period of limitations (usually 3 years), but keep employment‑tax documents for 4 years and special‑case records (bad‑debt, fossil‑fraud, etc.) for their specified longer periods. Always check the specific IRS rule that matches the record you need to keep.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
**Why you must keep business records**

| Reason | What it looks like in practice | Where the rule comes from |
|--------|------------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Proof for taxes** | Every time you file a tax return you need to show the IRS where the money came from and how it was spent. | The IRS requires that *“you must keep supporting documents that show the amounts and sources of your gross receipts”* and that those records “support the entries in your books and on your tax return” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12). |
| **To answer the IRS** | If the IRS reviews or “examines” a return, you’ll have to explain what you reported. Having a complete set of records speeds the process and reduces the chance of penalties. | “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS. If the IRS examines any of your tax returns, you may be asked to explain the items reported. A complete set of records will speed up the examination” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11). |
| **Track business money** | A daily record shows exactly how much cash entered or left the business, helps you spot mistakes and spot fraud, and lets you reconcile your bank account each month. | “Record expenses when they occur… you should deposit all daily receipts in your business checking account… When you reconcile your checking account, you will verify how much money you have in the account” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14). |
| **Legal and financial decisions** | Banks and lenders look at your income statement and balance sheet before giving you a loan, and they need a clean trail of income, expenses and assets. | “These statements can help you in dealing with your bank or creditors and help you manage your business” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11). |
| **Compliance with other rules** | Certain health‑and‑safety records and insurance documents must be held for a specific amount of time. | The OSHA section shows that injury records “are kept… for at least five years” and that some reports must be mailed within a few hours of an incident [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15). |

**Bottom line:** Keeping good records lets you:

1. file accurate tax returns that the IRS can audit,
2. prove where every dollar came from and went to,
3. manage day‑to‑day cash flow and avoid errors, and
4. satisfy lenders, regulators and insurers who need proof that the business is operating properly.

In short, documentation is the business’s “paper trail” that protects you and keeps your operations running smoothly.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. Accrual Accounting – The Basics**

| Feature | Cash Method | Accrual Method |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| When income is recorded | When money comes in | When it is earned (the event that creates the right to receive money has happened) |
| When expenses are deducted | When money is paid | When the expense is incurred (the event that creates the obligation has happened) |
| Typical use | Small, simple businesses; people who want a quick picture of their cash flow | Businesses that sell products or services, or that keep an inventory; anyone who needs to match what they earned with what they spent in the same year |

---

### 1.  How the different rules work

**Cash method**  
- Only counts money that actually passes through the bank or cash drawer.  
- A bill you pay next month is *not* an expense until you write the check or make an electronic payment.  
- You report income only when customers pay you.  

**Accrual method**  
- Income is matched with the period in which it is earned, not when it is received.  
- Expenses are matched with the period in which the related goods or services are received or performed, even if you pay later.  
- For an expense to be deducted you must satisfy two things:  
  1. The *all‑events test* – all facts that fix the liability are settled and the amount can be measured accurately.  
  2. *Economic performance* – the service or product has been delivered or used by you (or you have given it to somebody else) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

### 2.  A concrete example

| Situation | Cash method | Accrual method |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| You buy office supplies in December, pay in January | The $500 expense is deducted only in 2026, when you actually pay. | You deduct the expense in 2025 because the supplies arrive and you are liable for them in that year – all events have settled and economic performance is done, even though you pay later. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |

### 3.  Special rules that often make accrual the default

- **Inventories** – If you produce, buy, or sell merchandise, you normally must keep an inventory record. When you do, you *must use the accrual method for purchases and sales* because the inventory is part of the cost of goods sold. Small businesses can sometimes skip inventory records but still must use an accounting method that reflects income. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Related‑person rules** – If your business owes money to a related person who follows the cash method, you can’t deduct that debt until the payment (and the related income) actually happen. The rule is tied to whether the related person uses cash or accrual. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

### 4.  How cancellations of debt are treated

- **Cash method** – If a creditor forgives part of a debt, you *do not* have to add the forgiven amount to your income because it would have been a deductible expense when your cash was paid.  
- **Accrual method** – The forgiven amount *is* taxable income because the expense was already deducted when you incurred the liability. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=23)  

---

### 5.  When to choose each method

| Type of business | Likely method |
|-------------------|---------------|
| Sole‑proprietorship with no inventory, few
   receipts, mostly cash payments | Cash (simpler) |
| Retail store, manufacturer, or company that
   sells products on credit | Accrual (required if you keep inventory) |
| Service‑only business with no inventory and all
   clients pay in cash | Cash (if you want easy bookkeeping) |

---

**In short:**  
- **Cash accounting** treats money as it actually moves.  
- **Accrual accounting** treats money when it is earned or spent, regardless of when the cash changes hands.  
Each method has rules (like the all‑events test, economic performance, inventory requirements, and related‑person rules) that tell you which income and expenses belong in which tax year.  
If you’re not sure which method applies to your situation, the IRS index lists “cash” and “accrual” accounting rules on pages 14–15 and 32 of the tax guide, and the IRS explains the inventory requirement on page 13. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=54)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes – you can deduct the costs that are directly connected to a business trip, but only if the trip meets the IRS’s **travel‑away‑from‑home** rules and you keep good records.  

| What you can deduct | How it works | Key rule or limit |
|---------------------|--------------|-------------------|
| **Transportation to the destination** (air, train, bus, car, taxi, limo, etc.) | Full cost of the trip between your home and the job location | You must be “away from home” for more than a normal day (see [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)) |
| **Lodging** (hotel room, etc.) | Full cost if the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep/rest to do the job | Must be a legitimate business purpose (see [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)) |
| **Meals** | You may deduct 50 % of the cost or use the standard meal allowance. | Standard rates are set in Pub. 463; 50 % deduction is the usual rule (see [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)) |
| **Tips** | If you paid a tip for any of the above expenses (e.g., hotel, taxi) you can deduct it. | The tip must be paid for a service that is part of the deductible expense (see [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)) |
| **Telephone and other communication** | Money you spend on business calls while traveling. | Must be directly related to the business activity (see [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)) |
| **Transportation within the destination** | Fares for buses, trains, taxis, etc. between the hotel and the work site. | Deducted as part of travel (see [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)) |
| **Baggage and shipping** | Cost of sending luggage or sample/display materials between your home office and the travel destination. | Deductible if for business (see [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)) |
| **Parking and tolls** | Fees paid while the vehicle is used for business travel. | Deductible, but a vehicle’s insurance premiums are not (see [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)) |
| **Car/truck expenses** | If you use your own car, you may take the standard mileage rate **or** actual expenses (fuel, repairs, depreciation, etc.). | Split between business and personal use if you drive for both purposes (see [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)) |
| **Reimbursements to employees** | If you reimburse employees for travel or meals under an accountable plan, those amounts are deductible. | Follow Pub. 15 for reporting rules (see [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)) |

### How to determine if a trip is deductible
1. **Travel away from home**: You must be away from your “tax home” longer than an ordinary day’s work **and** need sleep or rest to perform your duties. The tax home is generally your normal place of business (see [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)).
2. **Ordinary and necessary**: The expense must be typical for your type of business and truly needed to conduct business (see [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)).

### Record‑keeping
To claim these deductions, keep receipts, mileage logs, or other documentation that shows the business purpose of each expense (see Segment 7).  

**Bottom line**: Yes, business travel costs that satisfy the "away‑from‑home" test and are ordinary/necessary are deductible. Keep detailed records, and divide any mixed‑purpose expenses appropriately.

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
**What to include in an Executive Summary**

An executive summary is the first page (or first few pages) of a business plan and gives the reader a quick snapshot of the whole proposal.  It should cover the most important parts of the plan so that anyone who reads only this section still understands what the business is, why it will succeed, and how much money it needs.

Typical items that appear in the executive summary are:

| Section | What to write | Where the idea comes from (in the provided segments) |
|---|---|---|
| **Business Overview** | Name, location, type of business, short history and the mission/vision. | The “Describe Your Business” heading explains what a business description should contain [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12). |
| **Products / Services** | A concise description of the main product or service, its unique value and planned future offerings. | The “Describe Your Product(s)” section lists the points that should be mentioned [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12). |
| **Target Market & Competition** | Who the customers are, market size, and how the business will stand out from competitors. | The “Describe Your Business” section stresses the importance of showing industry information and a sustainable competitive advantage [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12). |
| **Business Model / Operations** | How the product is made or delivered, key suppliers, location, and capacity. | The “Fac­ility and Equipment” and “Proprietary Information” parts give clues on what operational details to summarize [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12). |
| **Financial Snapshot** | Total financial need, use of funds, key financial projections (income, cash flow, break‑even), and any equity already invested. | The “Money” section breaks down the financial documents that should be in the plan and highlights the summary of financial need, projections, and break‑even analysis [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16). |
| **Milestones / Timeline** | Key future milestones such as product launches, hiring plans, or opening dates. | While not spelled out verbatim, “Describe Your Business” says to project future projections and accomplishments in the first years [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12). |
| **Ask** | If you’re writing for investors or lenders, state the exact amount you are seeking and why it will be used. | The “Summary of Financial Need” in the “Money” section explains this request [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16). |

**Why it matters**

* It is the section most readers skim first.  
* It tells investors or lenders whether the business is worth looking at further.  
* It sets the tone for the rest of the plan—you should keep it concise, factual, and compelling.

**What the provided segments tell us**

The business‑plan guide gives the building blocks that an executive summary condenses: a clear business description, product details, market positioning, operational plan, and a financial footprint.  The guide explicitly says the plan should include “historical financial statements, projections and a description of the start‑up costs” – all of which belong in a high‑level financial snapshot in the executive summary [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  

**Missing explicit rule**

None of the segments provide a *formal, numbered list* of executive‑summary items, so the exact wording and order can be adapted to the particular business.  What is essential is that the summary includes a compressed version of each major heading in the plan (business, product, market, ops, finance, and ask).



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
**How to describe your target market**

1. **State the niche your business serves**  
   • Explain who your “best customer” is.  
   • For a business market, identify industry, company size, location or how the product is used.  
   • For a consumer market, segment by demographics (age, gender), geography, lifestyle, economic status, or the benefits customers want.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **List the key characteristics of that customer**  
   − **Demographic**: age range, gender, income level, education, marital status, etc.  
   − **Geographic**: city, region, urban/rural, climate, proximity to your store or service area.  
   − **Psychographic**: interests, values, attitudes, lifestyle choices.  
   − **Behavioral**: buying habits, brand loyalty, product usage patterns.  
   These details show why the customer will choose your product/service.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Show the market’s size and potential growth**  
   – Use population data, industry sales figures, tax statistics, or other industry reports to estimate how many potential customers fit your niche.  
   – Forecast how that number might grow over the next 3‑5 years.  
   – Estimate the portion of that pool you expect to capture (market share).  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Connect the description to your business strategy**  
   • Explain how product features, pricing, distribution, or promotional tactics match the needs and wants of the target market.  
   • Highlight any unique selling points that specifically appeal to that segment.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Example (illustration)**  
   Suppose you’re opening a boutique coffee shop in a college town.  
   – **Target niche**: students and young professionals aged 18‑30 who value high‑quality espresso and a cozy, social environment.  
   – **Characteristics**: mainly single, monthly income $1,200‑$3,000, lives within a 5‑mile radius, values sustainability and local culture.  
   – **Market size**: 4,000 students and 3,000 young professionals in the area; projected 5% annual growth in young adult population.  
   – **Target share**: aim to capture 10% of that 7,000‑person pool in the first year, growing to 12% by year three.  
   • Your menu (specialty lattes, oat milk, vegan pastries), Wi‑Fi, and community events are all tailored to those preferences.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

**Quick checklist for a clear target‑market description**

| Element | What to include | Citation |
|---------|-----------------|----------|
| Niche | Industry/consumer type | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Demographics | Age, gender, income | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Geography | City, region, distance | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Psychographics | Lifestyle, values | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Behavioral | Buying habits, loyalty | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Size & growth | Population & sales data | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Market share | Your projected capture | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| Fit with strategy | Product/price/distribution match | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |

Use this structure to write a concise, data‑driven paragraph or table that clearly tells investors, partners, and employees who you’re serving and why your business will succeed with them.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
### Short answer If any barrier that stops a person who uses a wheelchair from entering, parking, or using your shop can be removed or made “readily achievable,” you must do it. The ADA Standards for Accessible Design (Title III) require that a business provide accessible routes, entrances, parking, and service counters whenever it is practicable. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) --- ## 1. What “readily achievable” means - **“Readily achievable”** is a judgement call for each business. - If removing a barrier (step, narrow door, tall counter, etc.) can be done with reasonable cost, time, and effort, it is considered achievable. - If it would need major structural changes that are not practical, you can deviate from the exact standards as long as doing so does not create a serious safety risk. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) --- ## 2. Typical barriers that you should check | Barrier | What you need to do if it’s present | Where the rule comes from | |---------|------------------------------------|---------------------------| | **Entrance** – a step, turnstile, or door that can’t be opened by a wheelchair | • Remove the turnout and leave a 32‑inch wide opening (or the widest possible).
• If the turnstile must stay, provide an accessible gate next to it.
• If you have another door, you can use that as an alternate entrance and label it “Accessible.” | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) | | **Outdoor barrier** – awning too low, curb too high, doorway too narrow | Remove or modify the obstruction so the path from the sidewalk to the door has no steps or steep slopes and has a firm, slip‑resistant surface. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) | | **Parking** – space too narrow, no access aisle, or a slope that’s too steep | • Designate at least one accessible parking space.
• The space must be 8 ft wide and have a 5‑ft (car) or 8‑ft (van) access aisle.
• Mark it with the universal symbol, keep it on level ground (max 1:50 slope), and ensure a 98‑in. clearance to exits. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) & [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) | | **Service counters** – too high or no clear floor space | • Provide a lower section that is 36 in long and ≤ 36 in high, and give a 30×48 in clear area in front for a wheelchair to pull up to.
• If that can’t be done, add a nearby auxiliary counter or a folding shelf. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | | **Other** – narrow aisles, fixed tables, high lids | Make aisles at least 36 in wide, clear enough for a wheelchair, and use detachable fixtures so the person can pass. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | --- ## 3. How to decide what to do first 1. **Make the business accessible from the public sidewalk / parking lot** – this normally means an accessible route, curb ramps, and a clear entrance. 2. **Then provide access to the areas where customers actually do business** – counters, check‑outs, restrooms, etc. 3. Once the main functional areas are open, address any remaining barriers (toilet stalls, drink fountains, public phones). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) --- ## 4. Bottom line If your shop has any of the common barriers listed above and you can fix them without extraordinary cost or effort, you are required to do so. The ADA is not about giving special treatment—it is about eliminating barriers so everyone can use your business freely. *If you’re unsure whether a change is “readily achievable,” consult a qualified accessibility professional or the local ADA coordinator.* --- ### Quick checklist for you - [ ] Does a wheelchair user reach the front door without climbing a step or passing through a narrow gap? - [ ] Are there at least one (and, if needed, more) accessible parking spaces close to the entrance, with a proper access aisle? - [ ] Are counters and cash registers set to ≤ 36 in high with a clear 30×48 in space in front? - [ ] Are the sidewalks, curb ramps, and interior paths free of obstacles and slide‑resistant? If you answered “no” to any of these, it’s time to make the necessary changes—because the ADA says you must (unless it’s truly not achievable). results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**Starting a business and keeping your taxes organized**

1. **Decide what kind of business you want to form**  
   * Pick a legal structure (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc.). The type you choose will determine some of the records you must keep.  
   * *Citation: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=28)*  

2. **Get a taxpayer identification number (TIN)**  
   * Most new businesses need an **Employer Identification Number (EIN)**. If you’re a sole proprietor who will use your Social‑Security number, that can work, but an EIN is a good “official” number for the business.  
   * *Citation: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)*  

3. **Set up a simple accounting system**  
   * Choose one of the two common methods: **cash** or **accrual**. The method you pick should show clearly the income your business earns each tax year.  
   * Keep a separate set of books for each business if you have more than one.  
   * Use a checkbook (manual or electronic) as the main source for entries, and keep supporting documents such as sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, and canceled checks.  
   * *Citation: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

4. **Keep an organized record‑keeping system**  
   * Store records by year and type of income or expense.  
   * If you use electronic records, the system must **index, store, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce** the data in a legible format that the IRS can read.  
   * The same rules that apply to hard copies also apply to electronic copies.  
   * You may destroy the hard copies as soon as you have a working electronic system and a proof that the system meets IRS requirements.  
   * *Citation: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

5. **Keep special records for certain business types**  
   * A corporation should keep minutes of board meetings.  
   * Other business types may need different special documents; check IRS rules for your specific structure.  
   * *Citation: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

6. **Maintain financial statements**  
   * Prepare an **income statement** (shows income and expenses for a period) and a **balance sheet** (shows assets, liabilities, and equity on a date).  
   * These statements help you manage the business and work with banks or creditors.  
   * *Citation: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

7. **Track where money comes from and where it goes**  
   * Identify each source of receipts so you can separate business income from personal or non‑taxable income.  
   * Record deductible expenses promptly to avoid missing them when you file.  
   * *Citation: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

8. **Use IRS resources to stay on schedule**  
   * **Publication 583** is a guide for starting a business and keeping records.  
   * **Publication 509** (Tax Calendars) tells you when to file returns and make payments.  
   * Look up specific forms (e.g., 1040‑ES for estimated tax, 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC for non‑employee income) as you need them.  
   * *Citation: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=28), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=1)*  

9. **Keep everything ready for inspection**  
   * The IRS may want to review your records. Having a complete, organized set of records speeds the process.  
   * Store records in a secure place (physical or digital) and keep them for the required time.  
   * *Citation: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

10. **Ask for help if needed**  
    * If you’re unsure about recordkeeping or form filing, contact the IRS or a qualified tax professional, or use the IRS online help pages.  
    * *Citation: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=1)*  

---

**Bottom line:**  
Start with a clear business structure and EIN. Pick an accounting method (cash or accrual) and set up a simple books system. Keep all receipts, invoices, and support documents in a tidy, indexed format—whether paper or electronic. Use the IRS publications for specific deadlines and forms, and keep your books up to date so you’re ready when taxes come due.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
**How to keep your employees safe and make your premises accessible**

| What you should do | Why it matters | Where it’s written in the handbook |
|--------------------|----------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Create a confined‑space program** – identify which spaces need permits, train attendants, have rescue gear, and test atmospheres before entry. | Confined spaces can hide fire, gas, or oxygen‑deficient air. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=68) |
| **Post clear signs** around confined spaces and anywhere a jump‑or‑step hazard exists. | Workers need to know the danger before they touch it. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=68) |

## 1.  How to write a business plan  

1. **Start with a clear outline** – use the sections people normally ask for.  
   * Cover page, optional table of contents, executive summary, business description,  
     management, market, financial (“money”) section, and exhibits.  
   * The guide lists these as the standard skeleton of a plan. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

2. **Build each section one by one**  

   * **Executive summary** – a one‑to‑two‑paragraph snapshot of the idea, the money you need, where that money comes from, and your short‑term goals. Write this last so you can capture the whole picture. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

   * **Business description** – describe the product or service, how it fits in the industry, and why it will stay competitive.  
     * Include a product section that explains marketability, purpose, uniqueness, and future plans.  
     * Discuss proprietary knowledge or technology and any patents or trademarks.  
     * Talk about regulations, licences, and where you are in that process.  
     * Detail your facility, equipment, manufacturing process (if any), and capacity.  
     * Mention operational needs like transport and utilities. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

   * **Market analysis** – show the total market, your target customers, competitors, and how you’ll promote and sell. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

   * **Management & organization** – present the structure, key people, and their roles. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

   * **Financial (“money”) section** – the heart of the plan for investors or lenders.  
     * List source‑and‑use of funds, three‑year income projections, cash‑flow projections, break‑even analysis, and key assumptions. These documents convince others that the business can pay back or grow. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

   * **Exhibits** – attach supporting documents such as resumes, contracts, floor plans, or product photos. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

3. **Draft, review, and polish** – keep the language simple, avoid jargon, and let a mentor or counselor read it if you can. The guide says the plan should be *unique* to your business, so add or drop topics as needed. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

---

## 2.  How to set up accounting for a business  

1. **Choose an accounting method** that shows your income for the tax year (cash or accrual). The method must be the same for all books. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

2. **Create a clear record‑keeping system**  

   * Keep a **summary of all transactions** in books—journal and ledger.  
   * Use the main business checkbook (or electronic equivalent) to record entries.  
   * **Support each entry** with documents: sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, etc. Organise them by year and type. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

3. **Separate records for each business** if you own more than one. A corporation must also keep board‑meeting minutes. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

4. **Electronically store records**  

   * Any electronic system must index, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce books in legible form.  
   * You may destroy hard copies if the electronic system is proven to work.  
   * The IRS can test your system, and you must cooperate. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

5. **Keep the following key documents**  

   * **Income statement** – shows income and expenses over a period.  
   * **Balance sheet** – shows assets, liabilities, and equity at a single date.  
   * These statements help banks, creditors, and you manage the business. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

6. **Track receipts and expenses carefully**  

   * Identify every source of receipts so you can separate business from personal and taxable from non‑taxable income.  
   * Record expenses as they occur to avoid missing deductions. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

7. **Account for drawings** – withdrawals you take for personal use should be recorded in a **drawing account** so they don’t appear as business income. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=29)  

8. **Prepare tax returns** using the same records that support your books. Keep them available for IRS inspection, because missing documentation can delay or complicate an audit. results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, you need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) in the following situations:  
- **If you pay wages** to one or more employees.  
- **If you file pension or excise tax returns.**  
- **If your business is a partnership, corporation, LLC, or any other entity type** that the IRS treats as a separate tax‑payer (see Pub. 1635).  
  If you are a sole proprietor with *no employees* and only a simple tax return, you can use your Social Security number (SSN) as your taxpayer identification number (TIN), but many sole‑proprietors still obtain an EIN for privacy, banking, and reporting purposes.  
  The EIN can be obtained online at IRS.gov/EIN, by phone, or by mail/fax using Form SS‑4.  Once issued, it is the number you’ll use on all future returns and other paperwork.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

**What accounting method is linked to the EIN?**  
The EIN itself does **not** determine or come with a specific accounting method.  You can choose either the **cash method** or the **accrual method** for your business, as long as the method consistently reflects income and expenses for each year.  If you later decide to change methods, you usually must get IRS approval (Pub. 538).  

There is no mandated “default” accounting method that automatically follows an EIN.  

[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Injury/Illness Records You Must Keep**

| Record type | OSHA form/s | What it records | How long you must keep it | Source |
|-------------|-------------|-----------------|--------------------------|--------|
| **Work‑related injury/illness log** | **OSHA Form 300** | Every injury or illness that is *recordable* (i.e., requires first aid beyond a simple bandage, results in days away from work, restricted work, medical treatment beyond first aid, etc.). | **At least 5 years** from the date of the incident (or the end of the year in which it occurs). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Detailed incident report** | **OSHA Form 301** | A more detailed description of each recordable incident listed on Form 300. | **At least 5 years** along with the Form 300 entry. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Year‑end summary of injuries/illnesses** | **OSHA Form 300A** | Annual total of all recordable injuries and illnesses for the calendar year. | **At least 5 years** (same period as the underlying Form 300/301 records). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical / exposure records** | Employer’s own medical records (e.g., first‑aid charts, work‑site medical treatment logs, exposure monitoring reports). | Retained for “the time period required for each specific type of record” (e.g., medical treatment records must be kept for at least the period required by the relevant health‑and‑safety standard or medical‑record law). | **Depends on the specific record**—typically the same 5‑year period unless a different rule (e.g., OSHA’s medical‐record policy) requires a longer retention. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

### Key points

1. **Keep the OSHA forms at the worksite** – they should be readily accessible until the five‑year retention period ends.  
2. **Record‑exempt employers** (e.g., businesses with 10 or fewer workers or in certain low‑hazard industries) may not be required to keep a Form 300 log, but the forms above must be kept if you are subject to OSHA recordkeeping.  
3. **Electronic vs. paper** – The forms can be electronically filed with OSHA (e.g., 300A by March 2 of the following year in certain large establishments), but the employer must keep all paper or electronic copies for the full retention interval.  

### Practical checklist

- **At the time of an injury**: fill Form 300 and, if required, Form 301.  
- **End of calendar year**: summarize all records on Form 300A.  
- **After 5 years**: you may destroy the OSHA Form 300, 301, and 300A records (provided no other legal requirement applies).  
- **Medical and exposure records**: keep them until the period mandated by the applicable OSHA standard or other law (often 5 years, but verify).  

If you’re still unsure which forms apply to your business, check the “partial exemption” rule in § 1904.1 or your industry’s specific requirements. If you find your injury records are incomplete or if you haven’t kept the documents for the required time, you could face OSHA penalties.
